## 보관 원문

> # Application of Electric Smelting Furnace to Ironmaking
>
> This open-access review distinguishes the submerged arc furnace (SAF) from the
> open slag bath furnace (OSBF). In an SAF, the arc is submerged in the burden or
> slag. In an OSBF, the electrode is positioned close to the bath and a short
> open or "brush" arc spreads heat over the slag surface. The review finds that
> many claimed OSBF advantages still rely on equipment-supplier information and
> lack independent quantitative validation.
>
> Electric smelting of DRI is not new. The review identifies hot-metal electric
> smelting operations at New Zealand Steel, Steel Dynamics and
> Highveld/Robusteel, but states that they do not operate at the scale required
> to replace a blast furnace. New Zealand Steel is reported to use two 50 MW
> rectangular furnaces with six in-line Söderberg electrodes, to produce about
> 0.6 Mt of steel per year, and to have produced more than 23 Mt of hot metal on
> the original hearths since the 1980s.
>
> Published operating examples produced hot metal containing roughly 3.2–4%
> carbon and 0.2–1.2% silicon. Laboratory electric-smelting results were reported
> at 2.5–4.5% carbon and 0.05–1.2% silicon. These ranges show why the ESF product
> is a BOF/EAF feed and not finished liquid steel.
>
> For low-quality cold DRI processed directly in an EAF, the review cites modelled
> slag volumes of 543–630 kg per tonne of liquid steel and approximately
> 651 kWh/t of specific electrical energy, compared with about 413 kWh/t for a
> scrap-fed EAF. The comparison explains the motive for separating gangue in an
> ESF; it is not an ESF electricity-consumption measurement.
>
> The review cites a modelled Scope 1 result of about 0.33 t CO2 per tonne of
> liquid steel for DRI–ESF–BOF, versus 1.954 t CO2/t for BF–BOF. The boundary
> assumes maximum electric heating, excludes electricity and upstream emissions,
> and excludes credits for recovered gas and cement use of slag. It must not be
> presented as a measured full-chain product footprint.
>
> Furnace architecture can be circular or rectangular, AC or DC, and can use
> graphite or self-baking Söderberg electrodes. AC furnaces typically use three
> electrodes; DC furnaces typically use one electrode and a conductive hearth.
> The choice affects rectifier cost, arc interaction, hot spots, maintenance and
> scale.
>
> The central unresolved issues are the balance between feed rate and furnace
> power, arc length and stability, slag thermal and electrical conductivity,
> heat distribution, refractory protection and roof radiation loss. Open-arc
> operation can increase roof radiation and refractory wear. Because the bath
> has no mechanical stirring, arc–bath interaction and heat transfer are key.
>
> Supplier scale estimates imply that two rectangular or three circular OSBF
> units may be needed to match the 2.5–4 Mt/y hot-metal output of a medium blast
> furnace. The review does not regard these estimates as independently validated.
> It concludes that OSBF technology has been demonstrated only at limited
> industrial scale and that independent scale-up data are still missing.
>
